content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
In recent years, the information bottleneck has emerged as a useful framework for understanding deep networks.
It provides a framework for theoretically motivating the choice of a intermediate representation T when learning to predict Y given X.  The constrained optimization required by the information bottleneck is often pursued using Lagrange multipliers.  Previous work by Kolchinsky, et al pointed out that, when Y is a deterministic function of X, the Lagrange multiplier technique breaks down, and also that solutions to the information bottleneck criterion are degenerate.  They proposed a simple modification to the objective arising from application of Lagrange multipliers that, in a sense, always "works", even in the case that Y is a deterministic function of X.  

This paper proves that a more general family of modifications of the Lagrange multipliers, in a sense, "work".   They also provide solid experiments supporting this theory.  They also show how the appropriate Lagrange multiplier depends on the amount of "compression" from X to T desired. 

The paper is very clear and very well-written.  The description of previous work is extensive, and interesting.  In a sense, proving that a more general family of methods work makes it clear why the method of Kolchinsky, et al worked.  Having a mapping from the desired compression level to the required Lagrange multiplier seems potentially valuable.

Generally, the contribution feels a little incremental and technical to me.  I would not argue against accepting the paper if others like it.

Answer to AnonReviewer #2
Dear AnonReviewer2,

We would like to thank the anonymous reviewers very much for their valuable comments! We realize that we have not sufficiently stressed the main contributions of the article:
    • The most important contribution of the article is the fact that we found the bijective mapping between the Lagrange multiplier and the level of compression. In the previous work (Kolchinksy et al. 2018) we only learned that this function existed. This distinction is very important in our opinion since our contribution has important practical implications: Now, in deterministic scenarios, we can solve the constrained problem $\max \lbrace I(T;Y) \rbrace \ \text{s.t.} \  I(X;T) \leq r$ with a single optimization of the convex IB Lagrangian instead of performing multiple optimizations to draw the curve and then find the best traded-off solution.
    • The extension from the squared IB Lagrangian to the convex IB Lagrangian is added for completeness, in order to make sure that the reader understands that many other Lagrangians have this property. We also stated it as a main contribution since it is exactly this extension that enabled us to find the bijective mapping.

Then, regarding the importance of computing these solutions in the deterministic case:
    • In many classification problems, the empirical distribution $\hat{p}_{XY}(x,y)$ found in the training/validation/test dataset usually reflects a deterministic relationship between X and Y. This is regardless of the fact that the true distribution might not reflect such behavior.
      For example, in the MNIST dataset, we have a collection of images x(i) that belong to a single digit class y(i). And this behavior also applies in many other datasets for different applications; e.g., object recognition (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100…), OCR (MNIST), Identity Recognition (CMU Face Images Dataset), Facial Recognition (Yale Face Database, CMU Multi-PIE Database…) and many others.
      Moreover, if the relationship between Y and X is very close to being deterministic, these issues still appear and need to be solved. In particular, when Y is ε-close to being deterministic as shown in Appendix C of (Kolchinksy et al. 2018).
    • Furthermore, these results apply in many other contexts rather than in deep (or more generally, machine) learning. For instance, in coding, quantization, compression, rate-distortion or channel coding. In the latter example, if Alice has access to X and communicates through a channel with capacity C to Bob, which wants to predict Y, then Alice should transmit the optimal bottleneck variable T which is adapted to the channel capacity (which can vary). In this case, to be able to explore the IB curve is very important, and since the channel can vary, to be able to realize a single optimization is also very important since it allows Alice to adapt its communication scheme rapidly.

References
Kolchinsky, Artemy, Brendan D. Tracey, and Steven Van Kuyk. "Caveats for information bottleneck in deterministic scenarios." ICLR, (2018).

content.title: Official Blind Review #1
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
In this paper, the authors introduced the convex information bottleneck Lagrangian. They want to provide a solution to the problem that when Y is a deterministic function of X, traditional IB Lagrangian can not explore the whole IB curve. The authors introduce a general family of convex IB Lagrangian, and prove that there exists a bijective mapping between the IB curve and IB Lagrangian multiplier. Several experiments are conducted to prove the performance of power IB Lagrangian and exponential Lagrangian.

The problem that IB Lagrangian multiplier can not explore the IB curve is worth understanding and fixing. However, the convex IB Lagrangian is not very different from the square IB Lagragians. Firstly, the authors didn't point out any deficiencies for using square IB Lagrangian, so the motivation of using other convex IB Lagrangian are not strong. Also, the theories about convex IB Lagrangian seem to be a simple generalization of the theories of square IB Lagrangian. Finally, the experiment results for square IB Lagrangian and exponential IB Lagrangian are quite similar. 

Therefore, the whole paper seem to be too incremental, compared to square IB Lagrangian. I think the contribution of this paper is not enough to be accepted.

content.title: Main contribution and relation to squared IB Lagrangian
content.comment:
Dear AnonReviewer1,

We would like to thank the anonymous reviewers very much for their valuable comments! We realize that we have not sufficiently stressed the main contributions of the article:
    • The most important contribution of the article is the fact that we found the bijective mapping between the Lagrange multiplier and the level of compression. In the previous work (Kolchinksy et al. 2018) we only learned that this function existed. This distinction is very important in our opinion since our contribution has important practical implications: Now, in deterministic scenarios, we can solve the constrained problem $\max \lbrace I(T;Y) \rbrace \ \text{s.t.} \  I(X;T) \leq r$ with a single optimization of the convex IB Lagrangian instead of performing multiple optimizations to draw the curve and then find the best traded-off solution.
    • The extension from the squared IB Lagrangian to the convex IB Lagrangian is added for completeness, in order to make sure that the reader understands that many other Lagrangians have this property. We also stated it as a main contribution since it is exactly this extension that enabled us to find the bijective mapping.

Finally, we would like to point out that our intention is not to argue against the squared IB Lagrangian. We show an important property of the squared IB Lagrangian (i.e., allowing a single optimization for solving the constrained problem the IB poses) and state (for completeness) that all other Lagragians with a function h that is monotonically increasing and strictly convex also have this important property.

References
Kolchinsky, Artemy, Brendan D. Tracey, and Steven Van Kuyk. "Caveats for information bottleneck in deterministic scenarios." ICLR, (2018).

content.title: Official Blind Review #4
content.review_assessment:_thoroughness_in_paper: I read the paper at least twice and used my best judgement in assessing the paper.
content.review:
The information bottleneck Lagrangian corresponds to the optimization problem max I(Y;T) - \beta I(X;T) over all T satisfying the Markov chain Y-X-T. Recent literature has shown that different values of \beta may correspond to the same value of I(X;T) at the optimum, or the same \beta may have multiple optimum values of I(X;T). This has motivated alternate versions of the Lagrangian where I(X;T) is replaced by a function of I(X;T). Building up on a recent suggestion to replace I(X;T) by I(X;T)^2, this paper looks at h(I(X;T)) for a strictly convex function h. The main result is that each \beta corresponds to a unique I(X;T) in this setting, thus generalizing the squared Lagrangian formulation.

The paper is well-motivated and the author's have cited relevant literature. The paper's contributions, although correct, are incremental in my opinion. The main observation of this paper is essentially contained in the squared IB result, and I don't think the jump from squaring to using arbitrary strictly convex functions is sufficiently novel. For this reason, I recommend this paper be rejected. 

Minor comments: I have some comments regarding the technical presentation. These have not influenced my decision, but may be useful in future iterations of the paper.

- Throughout the paper, the authors appear to assume random variables with finite, discrete supports. This is evidenced by their use of entropy as opposed to differential entropy throughout the paper. However, when I read the simulations section, the authors appear to use a continuous representation T. Is the theory valid for continuous representations T? 
- Related to above: What is the set \Delta in equation (1)? If it is as stated "the set of all random variables satisfying Y--X--T$, then there is no reason to expect a maximizer to exist. Is is more appropriate to use \sup in (1) since the existence of an optimizing T is not guaranteed.
- The notation used to depict distributions of random variables is archaic. For example, the authors use p(x) and p(y) for the pdfs of X and Y. This creates ambiguity: What is p(1)?  The authors should use more modern notation with pdfs denoted by subscripts of the r.v., such as p_X(x), p_Y(y), p_{Y|X}(y|x), and so on.

content.title: Main contribution and minor comments
content.comment:
Dear AnonReviewer4,

We would like to thank the anonymous reviewers very much for their valuable comments! We realize that we have not sufficiently stressed the main contributions of the article:
    • The most important contribution of the article is the fact that we found the bijective mapping between the Lagrange multiplier and the level of compression. In the previous work (Kolchinksy et al. 2018) we only learned that this function existed. This distinction is very important in our opinion since our contribution has important practical implications: Now, in deterministic scenarios, we can solve the constrained problem $\max \lbrace I(T;Y) \rbrace \ \text{s.t.} \  I(X;T) \leq r$ with a single optimization of the convex IB Lagrangian instead of performing multiple optimizations to draw the curve and then find the best traded-off solution.
    • The extension from the squared IB Lagrangian to the convex IB Lagrangian is added for completeness, in order to make sure that the reader understands that many other Lagrangians have this property. We also stated it as a main contribution since it is exactly this extension that enabled us to find the bijective mapping.

Regarding your minor comments:
    • Regarding the differential entropy: we agree that we committed an abuse of notation. In order to make it work for both continuous and discrete variables we made the following changes in the revision of our manuscript:
        - We replaced the statements that involved the entropies with more general statements with the mutual information so it is clear that it holds for both discrete and continuous random variables.
        - We replaced the Appendix D image (Figure 4) with a more general one so that it does not create any confusion.
    • Regarding the $\Delta$ set in Equation (1), it is indeed the set of all random variables T which satisfy $Y \leftrightarrow X \leftrightarrow T$. Note the Markov Chain $Y \leftrightarrow X \leftrightarrow T$ is enforced by the assumption that X and Y are related and since T is obtained through X. Moreover, this objective function is concave (Lemma 5 from Gilad-Bachrach et al. (2003)) and the search set is compact, hence it has a maximum. As you can see in the attached Figure  (https://gofile.io/?c=zAMdKf) the dark orange region corresponds to $\Delta$, which might or might not be compact, however, once we impose $I(X;T) \leq r$ the search set becomes compact (hatched region) and the supreme is the maximum.
    • Regarding the notation (i.e., using, e.g., $p(y)$ instead of $p_{Y}(y)$), we would like to thank the reviewer for pointing this out, and we updated the notation for making the text clearer.

References
Kolchinsky, Artemy, Brendan D. Tracey, and Steven Van Kuyk. "Caveats for information bottleneck in deterministic scenarios." ICLR, (2018).
Gilad-Bachrach, Ran, Amir Navot, and Naftali Tishby. "An information theoretic tradeoff between complexity and accuracy."Learning Theory and Kernel Machines. Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg, 2003. 595-609.
